div.head: II Cn 13
div.ab: ⁊ se ðe utlages weorc gewyrce, wealde se cingc þæs friþes.
Utlaga. Se ðe útlages weorc gewyrce, wealde se cyng ðæs friðes.
And se ðe útlages weorc gewyrce, wealde se cyningc þæs friðes.
Et qui opus útlagii fecerit, eius reuocatio sit in misericordia regis (pacis emendatio in solius regis consistat imperio).
Si quis fecerit opus expulsi, quod Angli uocant útlages ƿeorc, uideat rex de pace.
Et si quis exlegis factum fecerit, consideret rex de pace.
Utlaga. Se ðe útlages weorc gewyrce wealde se cyng ðæs friðes.
And se ðe utlages weorc gewyrce, wealde se cingc þæs friþes.
(Friedloser. B) Und wer Friedlosenwerk verübt: [da] verfüge der König über den Frieden [den jener sich wiederkaufe].
(Outlaw. B) And whoever commits a deed that incurs outlawry: let the king decide on his [being restored to the] peace.
Outlawry. If anyone does the deed of an outlaw, the king alone shall have power to grant him security.
And if anyone commits a deed punishable by outlawry, the king [alone] is to have power to grant him peace.
And the king has the power to grant clemency to those who engage in outlawry.
div.note: B's heading ‘Utlaga’ is red.; BR: added from Gesetze I p. 317, October 2026 (MS Cons)

utlagu, fm., setzt Toller, vielleicht nur hierher an. Ob -a, wie Price-Thorpe annimmt, Plural bed., ist für c. 1125 nicht sicher. ‘Ächtungsvergehen’ Schmid. Den No. utlaga (s. d. Wb) hat B dem Text entnommen, wie wiccean vor 4, 1

Toller posits utlagu, fem., perhaps only on the basis of this passage. Whether -a denotes a plural, as Price-Thorpe assume, is not certain for c. 1125. ‘Offence entailing outlawry’ Schmid. B took the nom. utlaga (see that word in Wb) from the text, as with wiccean before 4, 1
Vgl. Wb: utlah; die 2 Wörter sind Ein Nord. Begriff; Toller 1146b Z. 1
Cf. Wb: utlah; the 2 words form a single Norse concept; Toller 1146b l. 1
Vgl. Gl friedlos 17; Misericordia 4, was nur Normann. Ausdruck für die Verfügung des Richters über Leben und Vermögen des Verbrechers
Cf. Gl friedlos 17; Misericordia 4, which is only the Norman expression for the judge's power of disposal over the life and property of the criminal
i.e. a deed which would legally involve outlawry; cf. the Norse phrase göra utlaga verk.
Probably we are to understand ‘no-one but the king,’ cf. one MS of Q which reads, pacis emendatio in solius regis consistat imperio.
